FINAL ACTION
1.	The present application is being examined under the pre-AIA  first to invent provisions.
Preliminary Amendments and Status of the Claims
2.	The preliminary amendment filed 22 February 2022, in which the specification was amended and the sequence listing was provided, has been thoroughly reviewed and entered.
3.	Claims 1-20 are under prosecution.
Information Disclosure Statement
4.	The Information Disclosure Statement filed 28 February 2022 is acknowledged and has been considered.
It is noted that the listing of references in the specification is not a proper information disclosure statement.  37 CFR 1.98(b) requires a list of all patents, publications, or other information submitted for consideration by the Office, and MPEP § 609.04(a) states, the list may not be incorporated into the specification but must be submitted in a separate paper.  Therefore, unless the references have been cited by the examiner on form PTO-892, they have not been considered.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
5.	The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112(b):
(b)  CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor regards as the invention.
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph:
The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the applicant regards as his invention.
6.	Claims 1-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor or a joint inventor, or for pre-AIA  the applicant regards as the invention.
A.	Claim 1 (upon which claims 2-3 and 7-20 each depend) and claim 4 (upon which claims 5-6 depend) are each indefinite in the term “strong binding affinity,” which is a relative term which renders the claims indefinite.  The term strong binding affinity is not defined by the claims, the specification does not provide a standard for ascertaining the requisite degree, and one of ordinary skill in the art would not be reasonably apprised of the scope of the invention.
B.	It is also noted that none of claims 7, 10, 13-14, 16, or 17 utilize proper Markush language.  A proper Markush claim contains the language selected from the group consisting of A, B, and C.  See MPEP 803.02
C.	The recitations “(HCS),” “(IHC),” “(ICC),” “(ISH),” “(EIA),” and “(ELISA)” in claim 7 is indefinite because it is unclear if the text within the parenthesis is an alternative limitation of the claim or merely a descriptor of other elements of the claims.    In addition, the recitations are acronyms, the meanings of which may change over time, and the specification does not define what is encompassed by the term “CAPS.”
It is suggested the claim be amended to remove all parenthetical limitations and recite only full names or text for each limitation.
D.	Claim 9 (upon which claim 10 depends) is indefinite in each of the following:
I.	The recitation “the conjugation mixture,” which lacks antecedent basis because there is no previous recitation of a “conjugation mixture.”
II.	The recitation “the conjugates,” which lacks antecedent basis in the previous recitation of “binding moiety-oligonucleotide conjugates;” it is also noted that any amendments to the conjugates may affect the similar recitations at the end of iii) a).
III.	The recitation “the unconjugated first oligonucleotide sequence,” which antecedent basis because there is no previous recitation of an “unconjugated first oligonucleotide sequence.”
IV.	It is also suggested that the phrase “at least one first oligonucleotide sequence” in part ii) of claim 9 be amended so as to differentiate the limitation from “the first oligonucleotide sequence” of claim 1.
E.	Claim 11 is indefinite in each of the following:
I.	The recitation “the conjugation mixture,” which lacks antecedent basis because there is no previous recitation of a “conjugation mixture.”
II.	The recitation “the conjugates,” which lacks antecedent basis in the previous recitation of “binding moiety-oligonucleotide conjugates;” it is also noted that any amendments to the conjugates may affect the similar recitations at the end of iii) a).
III.	The recitation “the unconjugated second oligonucleotide sequence,” which lacks antecedent basis because there is no previous recitation of an “unconjugated second oligonucleotide sequence.”
F.	Claim 13 is indefinite in the limitation “the scaffold,” which lacks antecedent basis because there is no previous recitation of a “scaffold.”
G.	The term small molecule in claims 14 and 16 and the term “heavy atom” on claim 17 are a relative term which renders the claim indefinite.  The terms “small molecule” and “heavy atom” not defined by the claim, the specification does not provide a standard for ascertaining the requisite degree, and one of ordinary skill in the art would not be reasonably apprised of the scope of the invention.
H.	Claims 17 and 19 are each indefinite in the recitation “the hybridized detectable component,” which antecedent basis because there is no previous recitation of a “hybridized detectable component.”
I. 	Claim 17 is indefinite in each of the following”
I.	The recitation “the hybridized detectable component,” which lacks antecedent basis because there is no previous recitation of a “hybridized detectable component.”
II.	The recitation “the one or more signal generating moieties” in lines 1 and 2, which lacks antecedent basis because there is no previous recitation of “one or more signal generating moieties.”
J.	Claim 18 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), second paragraph, as being incomplete for omitting essential steps, such omission amounting to a gap between the steps.  See MPEP § 2172.01.  The omitted steps are:  how the automated system or robotic system is actually utilized in the method.
K.	It is suggested that the phrase “a second oligonucleotide sequence” in claim 20 be amended so as to differentiate the limitation from “the second oligonucleotide sequence” of claim 1.
L.	Applicant is cautioned against introducing new matter in response to the rejections and suggestions discussed above.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
7.	The following is a quotation of pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 103(a) which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
(a) A patent may not be obtained though the invention is not identically disclosed or described as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the subject matter sought to be patented and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious at the time the invention was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which said subject matter pertains. Patentability shall not be negatived by the manner in which the invention was made.
8.	This application currently names joint inventors. In considering patentability of the claims under pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 103(a), the examiner presumes that the subject matter of the various claims was commonly owned at the time any inventions covered therein were made absent any evidence to the contrary.  Applicant is advised of the obligation under 37 CFR 1.56 to point out the inventor and invention dates of each claim that was not commonly owned at the time a later invention was made in order for the examiner to consider the applicability of pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 103(c) and potential pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) or (g) prior art under pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 103(a).
9.	Clams 1-8 and 12-19 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over US 7,183,052 B2 Sorge (hereinafter referred to as “Sorge”) in view of US 2010/0159446 A1 Haff et al, (hereinafter referred to as “Haff”).
Regarding claim 1, Sorge teaches a method for assaying a target in a sample, comprising providing to the sample a probe comprising two nucleic acid subunits, wherein at least one subunit comprises a region which is complementary to a target nucleic acid sequence (col. 4, lines 28-31) and the other subunit comprises a signal generating moiety (col. 4, lines 40-43), binding or associating the subunits of the probe with one another in the absence of the target (col. 4, lines 35-37), and binding the target in the sample with the region(s) within the nucleic acid subunits which is complementary to the target (col. 5, lines 7-10).  Sorge goes on to teach that the subunits of the probe are associated with one another by hydrogen or covalent bond formation (col. 6, lines 14-16) and that 80-99% of the probe subunits are associated with one another under conditions used to bind target nucleic acid, which is sufficiently strong to prevent dissociation between the probe subunits (col. 4, lines 56-60; col. 16, lines 51-58), which reads on a 90% efficiency of conjugation of the probe subunits. (The examiner would like to note that the terms “nucleic acid” and “oligonucleotide” are used interchangeably throughout the disclosure of Sorge [col. 31, lines 50-52]).  Sorge also goes on to disclose that complementary nucleic acid sequences (which, in this case, would include the target nucleic acid sequence and at least one nucleic acid subunit comprising a region which is complementary to said target nucleic acid sequence) can anneal by the formation of hydrogen bonds between the complementary bases (col. 5, lines 53-56), which reads on the probe subunit having a strong binding affinity for the target.
Sorge does not disclose that flow cytometry is used to detect the signal generated from the binding of the target to the signal generating moiety of one of the probe subunits.
However, Haff teaches [0007] a method of assaying a target in a sample, comprising combining the sample with two probes, wherein the each probe comprises a binding moiety for the target that can be covalently associated with a oligonucleotide sequence and a product precursor that can be covalently associated with each oligonucleotide sequence, wherein the two oligonucleotide sequences are capable of hybridizing to one another and bind the target in the sample with the binding moieties of each probe, wherein the hybridization of the two probes causes a reaction between the first and second product precursors of the probes resulting in a detectable reaction product.  (In this case, the examiner interprets the reaction product precursors to be signal generating moieties which are indirectly detected by exposure of the reaction product to a detection system.)   Haff goes on to teach that the detection system comprises a detection component capable of interacting with said reaction product and an amplification component capable of producing a plurality of detectable moieties [0008], wherein the detectable moieties are detected using flow cytometry ([0084]; Figs. 29A and 29B).
It would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art to combine the teachings of Sorge and Haff in order to produce a method in which the binding moieties have a strong affinity for the target and in which the probes are at least 90% efficiently associated with the binding moieties and signal generating moieties and a person having ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to do so in order to optimize the detection method to prevent any dissociation of the target-probe system during the detection step of assaying the sample.  Additionally, it would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art to combine the teachings of Sorge and Haff to use a flow cytometry system for the detection of a signal generating moiety produced by the preceding optimized method, and a person having ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to do so since this technique is routinely used in the art to detect health disorders.
Regarding claims 2-3, the method of claim 1 is discussed above.  Sorge teaches that the first probe subunit comprising a region which is complementary to a target nucleic acid sequence and a second probe subunit comprising a signal generating moiety are combined together and bound prior to contacting the target nucleic acid contained in a sample (col. 4, lines 35-40).
Regarding claim 4, while Sorge and Haff teach as described above pertaining to instant claim 1, Sorge goes on to teach that the probe has at least two subunits wherein at least one subunit comprises a region or regions that are complementary to a target nucleic acid sequence (col. 4, lines 28-32) which would read on a probe having three nucleic acid subunits bound or associated with one another, wherein at least one subunit (which would act as an adapter) would bind the target nucleic acid sequence.
Regarding claims 5-6, the method of claim 4 is discussed above.  Sorge teaches that the subunits of the probe, which in this case would include the adapter subunit as described regarding claim 4 above, are associated or bound together prior to contacting the target nucleic acid contained in a sample (col. 4, lines 35-40).
Regarding claim 7, the method of claim 1 is discussed above. Sorge teaches a singleplex assay for the detection of β-actin wherein PCR amplification is utilized to measure a target present in the sample (col. 62, lines 25-35; col. 27, lines 10-13).
Regarding claim 8, the method of claim 1 is discussed above.  Haff teaches ([0163]; Figure 13) the preparation of oligonucleotide conjugates comprising complementary nucleic acid sequences and hemipeptides, (wherein the N-terminal hemi-peptide comprises the detectable component fluorescein [0158]), and wherein the oligonucleotide conjugates are first analyzed using HPLC, then purified using an analytic C-18 column, and subsequently analyzed using LC-MS.  While Haff does not specifically disclose that the resultant oligonucleotide conjugates possess 90% purity, the examiner believes that the purification and analysis of the oligonucleotide conjugates as taught in Haff would result in 90% purity of the oligonucleotide conjugates. It is noted that In re Best (195 USPQ 430) and In re Fitzgerald (205 USPQ 594) discuss the support of rejections wherein the prior art discloses subject matter which there is reason to believe naturally includes functions that are newly cited or is identical to a product instantly claimed.  In such a situation the burden is shifted to the applicants to prove that subject matter shown to be in the prior art does not possess characteristic relied on (205 USPQ 594, second column, first full paragraph).
Regarding claims 12 and 13, the method of claim 1 is discussed above. Sorge teaches that the labeled probe which comprises the second oligonucleotide sequence has an incorporated a specific binding partner, wherein said specific binding partner comprises a protein (col. 45, lines 26-64).
Regarding claim 14, the method of claim 1 is discussed above.  Haff teaches that the binding moiety is a protein [0043].
Regarding claims 15 and 16, the method of claim 1 is discussed above.  Sorge teaches that the target is serum (col. 19, lines 7-21), a biological target comprising a protein.
Regarding claim 17, the method of claim 1 is discussed above.  Sorge teaches that the signal generating moiety or the one or more signal generating moieties of one of the probe subunits comprises a fluorophore (col. 46, lines 8-18).
Regarding claim 18, the method of claim 1 is discussed above.  Sorge teaches that the method comprises the use of a PCR assay to detect a target nucleic acid sequence, wherein the reactions are assayed in an AB17700 spectrofluorometric thermocycler, which reads on an automated system.  Moreover, the examiner would like to note that In re Venner (120 USPQ 193,194) discusses the support of rejections wherein the prior art discloses a manual activity which accomplishes the same result as an instantly claimed automated or mechanical means.
Regarding claim 19, the method of claim 1 is discussed above.  Sorge teaches that hybridized nucleic acid subunits are removed from bound target nucleic acid, wherein said removal is by a washing process (col. 18, line 65-col. 19, line 1).
10.	Claims 9-11 and 20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being unpatentable over Sorge in view of Haff, as applied to claims 1 and 19 above, and in further view of Tyagi and Kramer, Nature Biotechnology, 14, pp. 303-308, March 1996,  (hereinafter referred to as “Tyagi”).
Regarding claims 9-11 and 20, the methods of claims 1 and 19 are discussed above in Section 9.
Neither Sorge nor Haff specifically teach that the preparation and isolation of the molecular probe and the detectable components or the re-probing of said sample with a second detectable component or plurality of second detectable components.
However, Tyagi teaches (“Synthesis of molecular beacons”, pg. 307, right col., last para.-pg. 308, left col., 1st para.) a method of preparing a molecular probe with a detectable component, comprising providing the oligonucleotide sequence capable of binding a target nucleic acid and the fluorophore 5-(2'-aminoethyl)aminonapthalene-1-sulfonic acid (EDANS).  Upon incubation of the mixture of the oligonucleotide sequence with the fluorophore EDANS, the reaction mixture was precipitated with sodium acetate and ethanol, thereby removing unreacted EDANS.  The resulting oligonucleotides which were then covalently bound to EDANS were then dissolved in triethylammonium acetate and fractionated using a C-18 reverse-phase column, wherein fractions absorbed at 260, 336, and 490 nm were isolated and assessed for characteristic fluorescence of EDANS.  Moreover, Tyagi goes on to point out (pg. 307, right col., 1st full para.) that their method of preparing a molecular probe with a detectable component allows for the detection of probe-target hybrids without having to separate them from unhybridized probes.  However, Tyagi does not specifically teach a 90% efficiency of the formation of the oligonucleotide conjugates (i.e., claims 9-11).
Tyagi also teaches that a single sample can be probed for several different targets using a method which comprises probing with a plurality of molecular probes, which are specific for different target sequences in the sample (pg. 307, right col., 4th full para.), wherein the probes can comprise a plurality of detectable components which can emit or can be excited by light at different wavelengths (i.e., claim 20; pg. 307, right col., 3rd full para.)
It would have been obvious to one skilled in the art that the precipitation of an oligonucleotide conjugate followed by the reverse-phase chromatography isolation of said conjugate, and a subsequent assessment of the isolated conjugate for characteristic EDANS fluorescence would ensure the isolation of a highly-efficient oligonucleotide conjugate.  It would have also been obvious to one having ordinary skill in the art that said isolation steps could be repeated until a desired efficiency of 90% was reached.  Moreover, it would have been obvious to one skilled in the art to combine the teachings of Sorge, Hall, and Tyagi to produce an oligonucleotide probe with the capability of binding a target nucleic acid and/or with a detectable component, and a person having ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to do so in order to produce highly-efficient probes which are extraordinarily target-specific, wherein Tyagi discloses (pg. 307, right col., 1st full para.) that the probes produced form their disclosure ignore nucleic acid target sequences that differ by as little as a single nucleotide.
Conclusion
11.	No claim is allowed.
12.	This is a continuation of Applicant's earlier Application No. 13/302,877.  All claims are drawn to the same invention claimed in the earlier application and could have been finally rejected on the grounds and art of record in the next Office action if they had been entered in the earlier application.  Accordingly, THIS ACTION IS MADE FINAL even though it is a first action in this case.  See MPEP § 706.07(b).  Applicant is reminded of the extension of time policy as set forth in 37 CFR 1.136(a).
13.	A shortened statutory period for reply to this final action is set to expire THREE MONTHS from the mailing date of this action.  In the event a first reply is filed within TWO MONTHS of the mailing date of this final action and the advisory action is not mailed until after the end of the THREE-MONTH shortened statutory period, then the shortened statutory period will expire on the date the advisory action is mailed, and any extension fee pursuant to 37 CFR 1.136(a) will be calculated from the mailing date of the advisory action.  In no, however, event will the statutory period for reply expire later than SIX MONTHS from the mailing date of this final action.
